title: WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS DEFEND THEIR FAVORITE PASTOR MORE FIERCELY THAN THEY DEFEND SCRIPTURE?
paragraphs: WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS DEFEND THEIR FAVORITE PASTOR MORE FIERCELY THAN THEY DEFEND SCRIPTURE?
When Loyalty to a Man Becomes Stronger Than Loyalty to Christ, the Church Is Already Standing on Dangerous Ground.
There is a kind of spiritual blindness that does not begin with someone rejecting Jesus.
Sometimes, it begins with someone loving their pastor so much that they stop questioning whether what he teaches actually agrees with the Word of God.
And the frightening part?
They still attend church. They still worship. They still raise their hands during prayer. They still quote Bible verses. They still believe they are defending the faith.
But somewhere along the way, something quietly changed.
The Bible stopped being the final authority.
The pastor became the final authority.
And nobody noticed when the throne changed occupants.
Read that again, because what follows may challenge something you have believed for years.
What happens when the man who taught you about Jesus begins teaching something Jesus never said?
What happens when the preacher who helped you survive your darkest season becomes the very person you are afraid to question?
What happens when defending your pastor starts requiring you to explain away Scripture, excuse wrongdoing, attack wounded believers, or silence anyone who asks for biblical accountability?
And here is the question that should make every Christian uncomfortable, including the person writing this:
If your favorite pastor and the written Word of God stood on opposite sides of an issue, whose side would you choose?
Not the answer you would give during Sunday worship.
The answer your actions would reveal.
Because sometimes the greatest test of our loyalty to Jesus comes when obeying Him costs us our loyalty to someone we deeply admire.
Imagine a woman sitting near the back of a church she has attended for fifteen years.
That church is where she learned to pray.
It is where her marriage received counseling during a painful season. Where her children attended Sunday school. Where she cried during worship after losing someone she loved.
And the pastor?
He was there.
He prayed with her. Encouraged her. Preached sermons that seemed to speak directly into her brokenness.
To her, he was more than a preacher.
He was a spiritual father.
Then one day, troubling allegations surface.
Perhaps it concerns money. Perhaps manipulation. Perhaps teaching that contradicts Scripture. Perhaps someone vulnerable has come forward describing serious mistreatment.
She does not know what to believe.
And she should not pretend to know what has not yet been established.
But instead of asking what is true, she feels something rise inside her.
Fear.
Because if the allegations are true, what does that mean about the church she trusted?
What does it mean about the sermons that helped her?
What does it mean about the years she gave, the sacrifices she made, and the spiritual family she loved?
So she begins defending him.
Before examining the evidence.
Before opening her Bible.
Before listening carefully to the people involved.
Before considering that a person can genuinely help others spiritually and still be capable of serious wrongdoing.
And suddenly, a troubling possibility becomes visible.
She may not only be defending her pastor. She may be defending the version of her own life that she cannot bear to question.
That is how spiritual loyalty can become entangled with fear, identity, gratitude, and belonging.
And if we are not careful, we can mistake that emotional attachment for faithfulness to God.
But Scripture does not leave us without guidance.
In Acts 17:11, Luke describes the Bereans with these Greek words:
“ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφὰς καθ’ ἡμέραν”
Anakrinontes tas graphas kath’ hēmeran.
Meaning, “examining the Scriptures daily.”
The full verse explains that they received the message eagerly while examining the Scriptures every day to see whether the things they heard were true.
Think about that.
These believers were examining the teaching associated with the apostle Paul.
Paul.
A man called by Christ. A man through whom God worked powerfully. A man whose apostolic teaching became part of the New Testament.
Yet the Bereans were commended for examining the Scriptures rather than accepting a message merely because of the messenger.
They were not condemned for asking questions.
They were called noble-minded.
The Greek word used to describe them is εὐγενέστεροι (eugenesteroi), meaning more noble or noble-minded in this context.
Their nobility was not demonstrated by unquestioning agreement.
It was demonstrated by an eager reception of the message joined with careful examination of Scripture.
That distinction matters.
Because biblical discernment is not rebellion.
And asking whether a sermon agrees with Scripture is not automatically dishonoring a pastor.
In fact, a faithful pastor should want people to know the Bible well enough to recognize truth, even when that truth exposes his own mistakes.
A shepherd who loves Christ does not need to become the center of everyone's spiritual universe.
He knows who the true Shepherd is.
Jesus said in John 10:11:
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say that every person claiming spiritual authority should receive unquestioning loyalty.
He identified Himself as the Good Shepherd.
Every earthly pastor is accountable to Him.
Every sermon must be measured against His truth.
Every ministry must remain subject to His lordship.
And every believer belongs ultimately to Christ.
This is where the issue becomes deeply personal.
Because some Christians can recognize idolatry when someone bows before a carved image, but struggle to recognize it when someone places a preacher beyond correction.
We know that money can become an idol.
We know that success can become an idol.
We know that relationships can become idols.
But a religious leader?
Someone who preaches Jesus?
Someone who has baptized hundreds, planted churches, or helped thousands of people?
Can admiration for that person become idolatrous?
Yes.
Not because respecting pastors is wrong.
But because any created person can become an idol when we give them the trust, allegiance, or authority that belongs to God alone.
The danger is not loving your pastor.
The danger is loving your pastor in a way that compromises your obedience to Christ.
The apostle Paul confronted something remarkably similar in Corinth.
Some believers were dividing themselves around preferred spiritual leaders.
One said he belonged to Paul.
Another to Apollos.
Another to Cephas.
Paul responded in 1 Corinthians 1:13 with a question that cuts through centuries of religious celebrity culture:
“Has Christ been divided?”
Then he asked whether Paul had been crucified for them.
The answer was obvious.
No preacher died on the cross to purchase your salvation.
No pastor rose from the grave to defeat death.
No ministry founder carries the authority of the risen Son of God.
And no church personality deserves the devotion that belongs to Jesus Christ.
Later, Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 3:5:
“What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.”
The Greek word is διάκονοι (diakonoi).
Servants.
Not saviors.
Not spiritual celebrities above examination.
Servants.
And Paul made the relationship even clearer in 1 Corinthians 3:7: neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything in comparison with God, who gives the growth.
This does not make pastoral ministry unimportant.
It puts pastoral ministry in its rightful place.
The preacher may plant.
The teacher may water.
The counselor may encourage.
But God gives the growth.
The moment we forget that, we begin giving human instruments the glory that belongs to the One who used them.
And sometimes, we do it without realizing it.
We say, “My pastor changed my life.”
Perhaps his ministry truly helped you.
Thank God for that.
But remember who gave the grace.
Who opened your heart.
Who convicted you of sin.
Who offered you forgiveness.
Who rescued you from darkness.
The pastor may have been the messenger.
Jesus is the Savior.
Never confuse the hands that carried the message with the Christ who made salvation possible.
And yet there is another side to this conversation that we must handle carefully.
Not every accusation against a pastor is true.
Not every disagreement is evidence of false teaching.
Not every imperfect statement is heresy.
Not every difficult pastoral decision is abuse.
And not every person who publicly criticizes a church leader is acting from pure motives.
Scripture commands fairness as well as discernment.
First Timothy 5:19 instructs believers not to entertain an accusation against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.
That is a serious safeguard against careless accusations.
But read what comes next.
First Timothy 5:20 addresses elders who persist in sin and calls for public rebuke so that others may take warning.
The same passage that protects elders against unsupported accusations also requires accountability when wrongdoing is established.
Do you see the balance?
Biblical justice does not mean believing every allegation automatically.
But it also does not mean dismissing every allegation automatically.
It means seeking truth.
It means examining evidence.
It means refusing favoritism.
In fact, 1 Timothy 5:21 explicitly warns against prejudice and partiality in carrying out these responsibilities.
We cannot claim to honor the Bible while embracing only the verses that protect our preferred leader and ignoring the verses that hold him accountable.
That is not faithfulness.
That is selective obedience.
And selective obedience becomes especially dangerous when vulnerable people are involved.
Imagine someone finally gathering the courage to speak about spiritual manipulation or mistreatment.
Their hands are shaking.
They know what they might lose.
Their friendships.
Their church community.
Their reputation.
Perhaps even their family's support.
They are terrified that nobody will believe them.
And before their concerns can be carefully examined, someone responds:
“Don't touch God's anointed.”
Those words can sound spiritual.
But they can also be used to stop necessary questions before the truth is known.
The expression is often drawn from passages such as Psalm 105:15, which says:
“Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!”
In its context, the psalm recalls God's protection of the patriarchs as He preserved His covenant purposes.
It is not a blanket declaration that modern pastors are immune from investigation, correction, or discipline.
We should not turn a passage about God's protection into a weapon against biblical accountability.
Consider David and Saul.
David refused to murder Saul when he had the opportunity, recognizing the seriousness of harming the king whom God had anointed.
Yet David did not pretend Saul's actions were righteous.
He did not deny the danger Saul posed.
He fled from Saul's violence.
He spoke truthfully about his own innocence.
Respect for authority did not require David to remain defenseless before wrongdoing.
And in Galatians 2:11–14, Paul publicly confronted Peter because Peter's conduct was inconsistent with the truth of the gospel.
Peter was an apostle.
Yet his position did not make his behavior beyond correction.
If an apostle could be confronted when his conduct contradicted gospel truth, how can any modern pastor reasonably claim to be beyond biblical examination?
We must distinguish between honoring spiritual leadership and protecting spiritual wrongdoing.
Those are not the same thing.
Hebrews 13:17 teaches believers to obey and submit to their leaders, who keep watch over their souls and will give an account.
That verse matters.
Church leadership is not a meaningless position.
Faithful pastors deserve respect, cooperation, prayer, and encouragement.
But Hebrews 13:17 also reminds us that leaders will give an account.
To whom?
Ultimately, to God.
And 1 Peter 5:2–3 instructs elders to shepherd God's flock willingly and eagerly, not for shameful gain and not domineering over those entrusted to them, but by being examples.
The Greek expression μηδ’ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες (mēd’ hōs katakyrieuontes) warns against domineering over those in one's care.
The flock is God's.
The authority is stewardship.
The leadership is meant to reflect the character of Christ.
A pastor is not authorized to replace a believer's conscience with his own preferences or to demand obedience to commands that contradict God's Word.
And the church is not meant to become a place where the most influential voice is automatically treated as the voice of God.
Because when human authority is no longer accountable, the people most likely to suffer are often the people least able to defend themselves.
There is something especially heartbreaking about believers who have been taught that questioning a pastor means questioning God.
They may spend years confusing fear with reverence.
Silence with submission.
Emotional pressure with spiritual conviction.
And loyalty to an institution with loyalty to Jesus.
But Christ did not die to make you spiritually dependent on an untouchable human personality.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
First Timothy 2:5 says:
“For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
One mediator.
Jesus Christ.
Your pastor can pray for you.
He can teach you.
He can counsel you.
He can correct you from Scripture.
He can walk beside you through grief and suffering.
But he cannot replace Christ.
He cannot become the final judge of your standing before God.
He cannot demand the allegiance that belongs to your Redeemer.
And he cannot make an unbiblical teaching true simply because he delivers it with confidence, charisma, tears, or anointing language.
Sometimes a sermon is emotionally powerful because it is faithful to Scripture.
Sometimes a sermon is emotionally powerful because the speaker is exceptionally persuasive.
Those are not necessarily the same thing.
A trembling voice does not establish truth.
A crowded sanctuary does not establish truth.
A miracle claim does not automatically validate every doctrine.
A large following does not establish truth.
And a preacher's ability to make people cry does not prove that everything he teaches comes from God.
Galatians 1:8 contains one of the strongest warnings in the New Testament.
Paul says that even if he himself, his companions, or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel contrary to the one already proclaimed, that messenger is to be accursed.
In Greek, the word is ἀνάθεμα (anathema), expressing a solemn judgment or curse.
Consider the force of Paul's argument.
Not even an impressive supernatural messenger has permission to rewrite the gospel.
Not even Paul himself could legitimately proclaim a contradictory gospel.
How much less should any pastor today be treated as an authority above the apostolic message preserved in Scripture?
This is not a call to become suspicious of every preacher.
It is a call to become deeply rooted in the Word of God.
And that brings us to a painful question.
Why do some believers know their pastor's favorite sayings better than they know the words of Jesus?
Why can they remember every conference slogan but struggle to explain the gospel?
Why can they recognize criticism of their church leader immediately but cannot recognize a verse being removed from its context?
Why do they become furious when someone questions their pastor's teaching but remain strangely unmoved when Scripture itself is misrepresented?
There may be several reasons.
Some are grateful for genuine help they received through a pastor's ministry.
Some are afraid of losing their spiritual community.
Some have been taught that loyalty means never disagreeing.
Some have invested years, money, and identity into a church and find it painful to reconsider what they were taught.
Some have never been equipped to read Scripture carefully for themselves.
And some have gradually developed an attachment to a spiritual personality that has become stronger than their commitment to biblical truth.
We should recognize these possibilities without pretending we can read another person's heart.
Only God knows every motive.
But each of us can examine our own.
And perhaps that is where this article must become more than a criticism of other Christians.
Perhaps it needs to become a mirror.
Because the temptation to elevate human voices above Scripture does not belong to one denomination, one church tradition, or one kind of preacher.
It can happen wherever people place their confidence in a human leader without practicing biblical discernment.
It can happen in traditional churches.
In charismatic churches.
In evangelical churches.
In independent ministries.
In small congregations.
In enormous ministries with global audiences.
And yes, it can happen among Christians who pride themselves on being especially biblical.
Nobody is immune to spiritual pride.
Nobody is beyond the need for correction.
Not pastors.
Not teachers.
Not ministry founders.
Not Christian content creators.
Not even the person who writes an article warning others about these dangers.
If anything I teach contradicts Scripture rightly understood, Scripture must correct me too.
That is not weakness.
That is submission to the authority of God's Word.
And there is something liberating about realizing that your faith does not have to collapse when a human leader disappoints you.
Perhaps you once admired a pastor who later fell into serious sin.
Perhaps you heard a sermon that genuinely helped you, only to discover that other teachings from the same preacher were deeply mistaken.
Perhaps you defended someone before you knew all the facts.
Perhaps you attacked a person who raised a legitimate concern.
Perhaps you ignored warning signs because you were afraid of what acknowledging them would mean.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Your past gratitude does not require your permanent denial.
You can acknowledge that someone helped you without defending everything they have done.
You can appreciate a faithful sermon without endorsing an unbiblical teaching.
You can love your church without excusing its failures.
You can honor your pastor without surrendering your discernment.
And you can repent of misplaced loyalty without pretending that every good thing you experienced was meaningless.
God's truth is not threatened when human beings are exposed as imperfect.
Jesus is still Lord.
The gospel is still true.
The cross has not lost its power.
The resurrection has not been undone.
And the faithfulness of Christ does not depend on the flawless reputation of any preacher.
That may be exactly what someone reading this needs to hear today.
Because perhaps you are not merely disappointed.
Perhaps you are devastated.
You trusted someone.
You defended someone.
You believed someone represented Christ faithfully.
And now you are struggling to separate your experience with that person from your understanding of God.
You may be asking whether your prayers were real.
Whether your conversion was real.
Whether the Scriptures that comforted you were real.
Whether God saw what happened.
Please remember this.
A messenger's failure does not invalidate the truth of a message that genuinely came from Scripture.
And a leader's wrongdoing does not make Jesus guilty of that wrongdoing.
Christ does not become unfaithful because someone who claimed to serve Him acted unfaithfully.
Second Timothy 2:13 reminds us that even when we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.
That does not excuse sin.
It magnifies the reliability of Christ.
Your hope was never supposed to rest on a pastor's perfection.
Your hope rests on the crucified and risen Savior.
And this is where the gospel becomes breathtakingly personal.
Jesus knows what betrayal feels like.
One of His own disciples handed Him over.
Another denied knowing Him.
Others fled when He was arrested.
He was falsely accused.
He was mocked.
He was condemned.
He suffered at the hands of sinful human beings.
Yet He did not abandon His Father's will.
He went to the cross.
Not because humanity had earned His love.
But because of the mercy and grace of God.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had mastered discernment.
Not after we had stopped idolizing people.
Not after we had corrected every misplaced allegiance.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
That means the person who has idolized a pastor can repent.
The person who has twisted Scripture can repent.
The person who has spread an unjust accusation can repent.
The person who has knowingly covered up wrongdoing can repent.
The pastor who has sinned can repent.
And the wounded believer who has begun to doubt God's goodness can come to Christ with honest questions and pain.
But repentance must never be confused with escaping accountability.
Forgiveness does not erase the need for truth.
Restoration to fellowship does not automatically establish fitness for leadership.
An apology does not automatically repair the damage caused by abuse, exploitation, or betrayal.
And genuine repentance bears fruit.
John the Baptist called people in Matthew 3:8 to bear fruit in keeping with repentance.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance, involving a change of mind and orientation that expresses itself in a changed life.
Biblical repentance is more than public tears.
More than a carefully worded statement.
More than saying, “Nobody is perfect.”
It means turning from sin toward God.
Where wrong has been done, it calls for truthfulness, responsibility, and appropriate efforts to make things right.
In serious cases, that may include independent investigation, restitution, removal from leadership, and cooperation with civil authorities.
Grace is not the enemy of justice.
And mercy does not require victims to remain silent or unsafe.
Jesus is full of grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
John 1:14 describes the incarnate Word as full of both.
This is the Christ-centered balance the church desperately needs.
We must refuse the cruelty that condemns people without evidence.
And we must refuse the favoritism that protects powerful people despite credible evidence.
We must refuse gossip.
And we must refuse concealment.
We must honor faithful shepherds.
And we must remember that shepherds are accountable to the Chief Shepherd.
First Peter 5:4 calls Christ the Chief Shepherd.
That title should humble every pastor and comfort every believer.
Because the church does not belong to the loudest preacher.
It does not belong to the wealthiest donor.
It does not belong to the most charismatic personality.
It does not belong to the family that founded the ministry.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
Acts 20:28 speaks of the church of God, which He obtained with His own blood.
Think about the price of that belonging.
The church was not purchased with a pastor's reputation.
It was purchased at the cost of Christ's blood.
How dare we treat His people as though they exist to protect a human brand?
How dare we make loyalty to a personality the measure of someone's faith?
How dare we demand silence where Scripture demands truth?
And yet, we must also ask ourselves whether our own desire to expose wrongdoing is motivated by love for Christ or by the satisfaction of seeing someone fall.
Because discernment without love can become another form of pride.
Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak the truth in love.
Truth matters.
Love matters.
And neither gives us permission to abandon the other.
If your pastor is faithfully preaching Scripture, caring for God's people, receiving correction, and seeking to live above reproach, encourage him.
Pray for him.
Support him appropriately.
Do not make his work needlessly difficult through suspicion, gossip, or unfair criticism.
Pastors are human beings who carry real responsibilities, experience exhaustion, and need grace like everyone else.
But if a pastor's teaching contradicts Scripture, examine it carefully.
If credible allegations arise, seek a fair and appropriate process.
If people are endangered, prioritize safety.
If serious wrongdoing is established, do not confuse protecting a reputation with protecting the gospel.
And if a leader insists that questioning him is equivalent to questioning God, remember the Bereans.
Remember Paul confronting Peter.
Remember that Christ alone is the Head of the church, as Colossians 1:18 teaches.
Above all, remember that Jesus never asked you to choose between loving Him and obeying His truth.
He is the truth.
John 14:6 records Jesus saying:
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
Not merely a teacher of truth.
The truth.
That changes everything.
Because when you defend Scripture faithfully, you are not defending a religious document as though it were detached from Christ.
You are honoring the God who has revealed Himself through His Word and supremely through His Son.
Jesus Himself prayed in John 17:17:
“Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.”
The Greek is striking:
“ὁ λόγος ὁ σὸς ἀλήθειά ἐστιν”
Ho logos ho sos alētheia estin.
“Your word is truth.”
Not merely popular.
Not merely inspirational.
Truth.
And the church must never trade truth for popularity.
Not even when the person asking us to make that trade is someone we love.
So perhaps the question is no longer simply why some Christians defend their favorite pastors more fiercely than Scripture.
Perhaps the deeper question is this:
Have we become so afraid of losing the people who introduced us to Jesus that we are willing to compromise the words of Jesus Himself?
That is a painful question.
But sometimes the questions that expose our hearts are the very questions God uses to lead us toward repentance.
And maybe tonight, somewhere, a believer is sitting alone with a Bible open.
They have spent years defending a ministry.
Years repeating what they were told.
Years assuming that disagreement meant rebellion.
But now they are reading Scripture for themselves.
Slowly.
Carefully.
Prayerfully.
And something is changing.
They are not losing Jesus.
They are learning to distinguish Jesus from the human beings who speak about Him.
They are discovering that biblical authority is not the same as authoritarian control.
That spiritual maturity is not blind agreement.
That humility includes being willing to admit, “I was wrong.”
And that faithfulness to Christ may sometimes require a difficult conversation, an uncomfortable correction, or the courage to walk away from a harmful situation.
There may be tears.
There may be grief.
There may be relationships that change.
But there can also be freedom.
The freedom of knowing that no human being owns your relationship with God.
The freedom of studying Scripture without fear.
The freedom of appreciating faithful leaders without worshiping them.
The freedom of loving the church while refusing to excuse sin.
And the freedom of following Jesus even when doing so costs you the approval of people.
This is not a call to abandon the church.
It is a call to return to Christ as the church's true Head.
Not a call to despise pastors.
A call to honor faithful pastors without making them idols.
Not a call to become cynical.
A call to become discerning.
Not a call to celebrate scandal.
A call to bring what is hidden into the light with truth, justice, humility, and love.
Because scandal is not the end of the story when people turn to Christ in repentance and faith.
And grace is not permission to remain in darkness.
Grace calls us into the light.
Perhaps you have been defending someone because you were afraid to admit that you had been deceived.
Perhaps you have remained silent because you did not want to lose your church family.
Perhaps you have confused loyalty with obedience.
Or perhaps you have become so angry at failed leaders that you are struggling to trust any shepherd at all.
Wherever you are, there is an invitation greater than the argument.
Come back to Jesus.
Come back to His Word.
Come back to the cross.
Come back to the gospel that does not depend on celebrity, influence, money, or human perfection.
And if this has exposed something in your own heart, do not rush past it.
Take a moment before God.
Ask Him to show you where admiration may have become misplaced devotion.
Ask Him for wisdom to recognize faithful teaching.
Ask Him for humility to receive correction.
Ask Him for courage to speak truth without cruelty.
Ask Him for compassion toward wounded believers.
And ask Him to make you more loyal to Christ than to any human name.
And if you have experienced God's grace after a season of spiritual confusion, your testimony may encourage someone else who feels trapped between faith and disappointment.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who desperately needs this message.
A believer afraid to ask questions.
A pastor who needs a loving reminder that leadership is stewardship.
A church member who has confused loyalty with silence.
A wounded Christian who has begun to believe that the failures of people mean the failure of Christ.
But before you leave, I want to share something important about why Gospel Warrior exists.
This ministry is not meant to build unquestioning loyalty to a personality.
It exists to point people to Jesus Christ.
To help people open their Bibles.
To confront sin without abandoning grace.
To comfort the wounded without compromising truth.
To encourage repentance, forgiveness, healing, and genuine spiritual transformation through the gospel.
These resources are intended to help people study, reflect, and become more firmly grounded in biblical truth.
Not because God's favor can be purchased.
Not because you owe money to a ministry in exchange for spiritual growth.
Rather, because voluntary, cheerful support can be a meaningful way of participating in gospel-centered work.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that each person should give as decided in the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Philippians 4:15–17 also shows that believers can participate in the work of gospel ministry through generous financial partnership.
Paul valued their gifts, yet he emphasized the spiritual fruit of their generosity rather than treating financial support as a purchase of God's approval.
That is the spirit in which I invite you.
Some may prayerfully view this as part of their offerings toward gospel work, while continuing to honor their responsibilities to their families and local congregations.
These items are simply an expression of appreciation. The greater purpose remains the ministry of God's Word and the encouragement of people to follow Christ.
You can still be part of this mission.
Pray for the ministry.
Read and examine the Scriptures.
Point people to the free library.
Speak about Jesus with someone who needs hope.
Financial giving is one way to support gospel work, but it is not the only way to glorify God.
What matters is that everything we do is offered in faith, love, and obedience to Christ.
First Corinthians 10:31 reminds us to do all things to the glory of God.
And that includes how we give, how we speak, how we share, how we treat wounded people, how we honor our pastors, and how we defend the truth.
The purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to gather people around another untouchable human voice.
It is to help people become more deeply rooted in the One whose voice is worth following above all others.
Jesus Christ.
The Good Shepherd.
The crucified Savior.
The risen King.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who heals the brokenhearted.
The One who calls His people out of darkness into His marvelous light.
The One who can restore what sin has shattered without ever calling evil good.
And when the applause fades, the scandals are forgotten, the famous names disappear, and every earthly ministry reaches its end, one truth will remain.
Jesus Christ is still Lord.
So love your pastor.
Pray for your pastor.
Encourage your pastor.
Honor faithful spiritual leadership.
But never give any pastor the throne that belongs to Jesus.
Never defend a human reputation by sacrificing biblical truth.
Never make your spiritual identity depend on the perfection of another sinner.
And never forget that the Shepherd who gave His life for you is worthy of greater loyalty than every preacher who has ever spoken His name.
Because when everything else falls apart, the question will not be whether you defended your favorite pastor well enough.
The question that matters most is whether you truly belonged to Christ.
The hands that first pointed you toward Jesus may fail you. But the nail-scarred hands that saved you will never lose their power to hold you.
